headline: Jeffrey's Ledge at 190 feet: cod tight to gravel, haddock scattered on the mud
subhead: A steady week on the ledge complex with groundfish holding to structure and the first bluefin sign showing on top as bait tightens up.
body_markdown:
One-ninety feet of water on the east side of Jeffrey's Ledge tells you almost everything you need to know this week. Drop a marker there and the sounder shows two different worlds inside a quarter mile — hard gravel humps holding cod tight to bottom, and softer mud basins off to the side stacked with haddock sitting a few feet up off the floor. That split has been the story of the whole week, and it's the story that should hold into the weekend.

Gravel and mud aren't just bottom types out here, they're two different fisheries. Cod want the hard stuff — broken gravel, cobble, the transition edges where current sweeps bait against structure. Haddock want it softer, working the mud basins and the flatter grounds where sand fleas and worms concentrate. Jeffrey's has both inside a short run, which is why boats working it this week have been able to switch programs mid-drift instead of running miles to change species.

Weather's cooperated. Light southwest breezes, working tides, and clean green water on the ledge have kept boats out and drifts controllable — that matters more than people think, because a two-knot drift on the gravel puts your jig past the strike zone before it ever gets seen. Slower drift days have produced better, cleaner cod bites; the days with more push have leaned haddock, since those fish will chase a bait a little further off bottom.

Tactically it's been jigs and bait both working, depending on what the boat's targeting. For cod on the gravel, a 12- to 16-ounce diamond jig tipped with a strip of squid, worked with a short lift-and-drop right on bottom, has been the go-to — cod on the ledge this time of year don't want to chase, they want it presented slow and right in their face. Clam and herring chunk baits fished on a high-low rig, weight just ticking bottom, have also been picking off cod along the gravel edges where the current sweeps scent downcurrent into the structure.

Haddock over the mud have been coming on smaller jigs — 6- to 8-ounce, fished a few cranks up off bottom with a slow, steady retrieve rather than an aggressive jig stroke. Haddock feed up, not down, so working a bait or jig 3 to 6 feet off the mud has out-produced anything worked tight to the bottom this week. Clam bait on a bottom rig still takes its share too, especially on the slower tide stages when the fish aren't as willing to move for a jig.

Pollock have been mixed in over the higher relief pinnacles closer to the western edge of the ledge and around structure toward Platts Bank, holding up higher in the water column — 60 to 90 feet down over bottom pushing 150 to 180 — and they'll hit the same diamond jigs meant for cod if you let them flutter on the fall instead of working them tight to bottom. Mackerel schools have been showing on the sounder in patches across the ledge and out toward Tillies Bank, which is exactly the kind of bait signature that starts pulling attention from bigger fish.

That's the piece worth watching. We flagged the pattern building a couple weeks back — mackerel and bait tightening up on structure tends to draw bluefin activity before the real fall push arrives, and there's been scattered word of tuna showing on top over the ledge chasing bait, nothing sustained yet, more scouting behavior than a pattern boats can plan a trip around. It's early. The giants that make October worth circling on the calendar haven't shown in numbers, but this kind of surface activity in late August is the leading edge of that, not a fluke. Worth keeping a rod rigged and ready if you're already out there for groundfish, but not worth running offshore specifically for yet.

Scantum Basin has been holding its usual late-summer mud character — haddock scattered through there in decent numbers but not concentrated, which matches the broader read on the ledge complex right now: this is a solid, workable bite, not a blowout. Boats that put in the time on the right bottom and match their presentation to gravel versus mud have had good mixed bags. Boats running one program everywhere have had spottier results.

Looking at the next few days, the moon's building and tidal push should sharpen up, which typically tightens the bite windows rather than killing them — expect shorter, more defined pushes of activity around the tide changes rather than an all-day grind. If the wind holds out of the southwest in the 8 to 12 knot range like it's been running, drift control stays manageable and boats should keep splitting time efficiently between the gravel for cod and the mud basins for haddock. If it swings more westerly or picks up, I'd lean toward the gravel humps first thing, since cod tend to hold tighter and feed more predictably when conditions get a little sloppier on top. Either way, the ledge is fishing the way it's supposed to for late August — steady, structure-dependent, and worth the run if you're willing to work both bottom types instead of anchoring on just one.
